projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with W.K. Manchette was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: What year did you go into the Army?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: I was drafted in January of 1942 into World War 2.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: Where were you living at the time?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: In Evansville.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: Indiana?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: Evansville, Indiana.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: Did you pick the service branch you joined?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: No, I was placed there through the draft.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: Do you recall your first days in service? What were they like?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: Well, it was quite a, you know, different life style. I was raised on a farm outside of Evansville, and so we went immediately into basic training and -- different life style.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: Were they real strict?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: Oh, yes. Basic training is always very strict.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: Do you remember your instructors?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: I can remember our first sergeant and basic trainees never forget their first sergeant. Leonard F. Schenecky (ph), and he was a very strict disciplinarian.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: What are some of your experiences at boot camp, training camp?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: Those that I remember, it was a three-month series and I recall the 25-mile forced march and also going through the live ammunition barbed wire. As they were firing over the top of you, you had to crawl I think about a hundred yards. And of course there were a lot of physical training. One of the things, you never did throw anything on the parade grounds or on the ground around the camp. And I can remember a few gentlemen who smoked, and I never did, but they would toss a cigarette butt and they would have to dig a hole three foot deep then and bury it. And a couple times like that and they didn't litter the area anymore.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: I'll bet. Which wars did you serve in?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: I served three and-a-half years, World War 2, and two years in the Korean War.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: Where exactly did you go?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: I was, in World War 2 I was here in the states all but six months. And I was in Army Specialized Training Program and was quartered in two universities, Kansas State College and University of Wisconsin. And at the end of those two and-a-half years I was sent over to Italy for six months, and then back, and I was discharged shortly after that. I had my three and-a-half years in there. Following that I applied for dental school. I had attended Evansville College before going into the service. I applied to dental school at St. Louis University and to get federal aid, and I didn't have any money, so I applied for the program that they had using my G.I. Bill of Rights. But to get maximum aid I had to give the Army two more years after I graduated. So that I did. And that's the reason I ended up going to Korea, because I graduated in dental school June of 1950 and that's when the Korean War broke out. So in September of I was back on the ship headed for Korea and I was there eighteen months.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: When you first arrived in Italy what was it like?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: I was attached at that time to 171st Evacuation Hospital and so it was not bad. We landed in Naples. And the Germans, they were retreating, so we followed the Germans for six months at the peninsula. And the war ended and I was right at the Czechoslovakian border -- Yugoslavian border. So we went the full length of it.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: What was your job or assignment?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: Surgical technician. I aided in surgeries and administered a lot of medications and gave shots and took blood pressures and things like that working in the evacuation hospital.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: You must have seen some pretty bad stuff.

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: We did. We saw all manners of wounds and injuries and things like that.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: Did you see any combat, you yourself?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: Never saw any combat. We were within artillery range and one time there was a round that landed right at the edge of our compound, but no one was injured.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: That's good.

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: By this time the Germans were in full retreat.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: What were some of your most memorable experiences?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: I think probably the most memorable was at the Po Valley, the Po River. We had bombed out all the bridges and the retreating Germans, when they came to the Po River, couldn't cross. So for many, many miles before we got to the Po, there was abandoned German equipment. And there were guns and tanks and all along the sides of the road there were just thousands of German prisoners. And there were just fields full of them. And we, of course, when we got there, we had some pontoon bridges thrown up. So that was a memorable experience. Another memorable experience was following close to a battle. I was in town with two other soldiers and we saw small Italian boys, about twelve years old, having gotten some German hand grenades. And they were throwing those hand grenades in canals and killing fish. Amazing that they didn't get hurt. Of course, many of them did, but we didn't see any of them get hurt. But they were using leftover German war materials, you know, like that. They had guns and rifles. Kind of an interesting time.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: Okay. What were your ranks?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: I was classified as a cadet through most of World War 2 because I was a student and working in the Army Specialized Training Program. Then at my senior year in dental school I was commissioned second lieutenant. And then when I graduated I was commissioned first lieutenant. And then after a year I was commissioned captain. And then a year later I was discharged.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: How did you stay in touch with your family?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: Letters. We wrote letters frequently. That was a soldier's chore most evenings when we got in.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: To write letters?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: To write letters, and hope we got letters from home. Very important.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: Was it hard for the letters to get through? Were there any delays or anything?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: No, not really.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: What was the food like?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: Good. I never had Army food that was bad. I came out of The Depression and so we didn't have a whole lot to eat that was quality food. So military food to me was good.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: Did you have plenty of supplies?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: Oh, yes. We never ran short.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: Did you have any pressure or stress? Were you scared?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: Oh, every once in a while you were scared, but we were really not fired upon so I really didn't get into that kind of fear. I don't know how I would react had I been in the front lines when the firing was going on.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: Did you do anything special for good luck or to make yourself feel better or anything like that?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: I had regular time of prayer. I always felt led to do that.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: Was it hard to keep your faith during the war?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: No, it wasn't. No problem there at all.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: Did the other men join in when you had prayer time?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: We would have frequently a chaplain on Sunday morning if we could, you know. If we weren't under stress, we had services. So when I was in Italy there were, oh, a number of times that we had church services. It was a multifaith service. Everyone joined in. Maybe one or two Sundays a month we could.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: How did folks entertain themselves?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: Played a lot of cards, told a lot of stories, sat around and talked. Football we played. We threw footballs and we played baseball. Checkers, played a lot of checkers.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: Did anyone ever come and entertain you all, like sometimes they have people go around and sing?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: No. When I was in Italy we had no entertainment.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: Did you get any leave when you were in Italy?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: No, I got no leave until it was time to come back to the states after the war.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: Did you travel anywhere besides Italy during World War 2? You went all the way up to Yugoslavia, you said, right?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: Yes, I went from Naples up to Gorizia. It was a town right at the border of Yugoslavia. That's a pretty fair trip. I would say probably as much danger as I ever got in Italy was riding in the back of those trucks through the mountains because the roads were quite hazardous and sometimes we were in a hurry. And there were a number of accidents and at times we were just a bit scared. But that was probably the most dangerous time of my journey.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: Do you recall any funny or unusual events?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: Well, not funny, but unusual. One time they brought a German prisoner. He was about my age. He had been captured, but he was wounded so the American medics took care of him and he was in my ward. And his name was Karl. And he had pictures of his wife and his children and I had a picture of my girlfriend. And I could speak just a little German. He could speak just a little English. So we had quite a, you know, developed quite a friendship. I often wondered whatever happened to him.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: How old were you at this time?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: Let's see, I was probably twenty.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: And he was your age then?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: Yes, yes.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: Okay. Did you guys ever pull any pranks on each other?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: Well, yes, there were always pranks, just recalling them. Oh, yes, one very amusing prank. We had a, and I was still here in the states, we had a fellow who was always irritating everybody. And I think every unit has one or two of those. And one night I was stationed in Manhattan, Kansas, and a tremendous blizzard came up. Well, this fellow had gone to sleep early and he was in his bed. So four guys, he had blankets pulled up over him, four guys picked him up, walked him out in the blizzard. You know, he was asleep in his bed. He never knew it. And just left him in the snow. And about three or four minutes later here he came in covered with snow. We often wondered what he felt like when awakened and snow blowing in his face. But he wasn't easy to get along with for a few days.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: Did you take a lot of photographs?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: What did you think of your fellow officers and soldiers?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: I think that they were a good group of people. Different. I was much surprised to find the difference in people from rural Indiana being billeted with people from New York and Chicago. It was a culture shock but it was educational. The war was a good experience for me.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: You don't regret that you were drafted at all?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: No. I think being drafted in the military and then being able to receive the benefits of the G.I. Bill of Rights, it paid for most all of my college. It was to me a blessing. To most people, it was not. But there are some good things that have come out of that Army. And I know in my dental school class, I guess oh, 75 percent of the men who were in school were on the G.I. Bill of Rights. They were veterans. So that veterans program caused a lot of people to be able to graduate from college. I was one of them.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: Do you remember D-Day?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: Yes, I sure do.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: What was that like?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: It was just exciting, almost like today has been with the people shouting, you know, in Iraq. At least things were going, and we were glad to see as being able to carry the war in that direction and to that extent. It was a joyous day.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: I bet. Do you recall the day your service ended?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: Yes, I do. I can recall being discharged and I'm talking about World War 2 now. Fort Bragg, North Carolina, I had been sent back there. I was working on the medical staff. And when my time came to be discharged, it was just a pretty good feeling to get back into civilian life and pursue life again.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: And the G.I. Bill paid for your college or most of it?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: The G. I. Bill of Rights paid for all my tuition, all my laboratory supplies and gave us thirty dollars a month for living expenses. It quite thoroughly paid for my entire education.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: Did you stay close with any of the men from your Army days?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: From the Korean conflict, yes, I still have one or two patients who come in to see me regularly. We happened to meet in Korea. And this gentleman lives in Henderson, Kentucky area. And we became friends then. And he knew I was a dentist. And when he got back he looked me up. And so it's been a fifty-year friendship.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: How long were you in Korea?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: Eighteen months.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: Did you fight there?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: No, I was a dentist. But when I first got to Korea, things were kind of critical and I was pressed into service as a compound commander of a prisoner of war camp. And I was in relative charge of about twelve hundred North Korean and Chinese prisoners of war. And so I worked at that camp for, I guess, four or five months.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: What was the camp like?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: We set it up. We had requisitioned squad tents. We set up several tents for the cooking of food, for toilet requirements and hospital surgical tents. But we also had billets, which was this abandoned building that we'd taken over. And we put cots and whatever was needed for the prisoners of war. We put them up and it was just a matter of overseeing the running of the camp. The prisoners of war did most all the work.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: So while you were in Korea those were the last years of your military? You got out right after the Korean Page 12 War?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: Yes, got out in June of 1952.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: And you were a dentist most of the time?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: Yes, yes.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: Did your military experience influence your thinking about war or the military in general?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: It didn't change my concepts very much at all. War is really a horrible thing. It's necessary at times. Korean War and in World War 2 it was very essential. And there's a price to be paid. And I knew that going in. And all of us, we didn't know if we'd get back. And you kind of live with that fear. You might call it fear. But as young men, you don't think too much about it. So as far as changing me in my overall philosophy and concept of life, other than broadening me and being educational, no, it didn't change me.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: Are you in any veterans organizations?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: How did your experience affect your life?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: I have become quite appreciative of everything. Freedom isn't free. Freedom is paid for and purchased by much sacrifice. I see the peace and the safety in American. And on foreign shores I have seen where that does not exist. So it has made me most grateful for America and for the fact that we are a nation that has great freedom. As I have seen the rest of the world, I have come to appreciate that more and more.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: What are your most vivid memories from World War 2 or the Korean War? Like, do you remember Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: Oh, yes. I remember Pearl Harbor. I was a senior in high school. And we didn't have television and many people didn't have radio. We were a very rural family. So I had gone to school that morning, quite a small country school, forty-eight in all four grades of high school. And that morning prior to classes taking up, a group of us boys were standing by a radiator and our superintendent came in. And he said, "Pearl Harbor has just been bombed." And he said, "We are in war." And he said, "You young men," and I was eighteen at the time, he said, "You are prime candidates." He said, "You're not going to be around here very long."

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: How did that make you guys feel?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: Expected it. As soon as he said war, we knew our ages, a little apprehensive. But they bombed Pearl Harbor. We were ready to go.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: How long after that were you drafted?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: Well, I was supposed to have been drafted in September of that same year, but I got a deferment because I was Page 14 already enrolled out at Evansville College and they let me finish my semester there. And then in January of '43 I was then drafted and went into active service.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: What about the Korean War? Any big days that stick out in your mind?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: Well, one of the big days of the Korean War, I was stationed at Puson and I was able after a few months to set up a clinic, dental clinic in Puson. And I would have some free time. And forty miles from Puson a big battle had occurred. A group of North Koreans had come down and ambushed an American combat unit. They had several tanks and artillary pieces. And so we went over there. And it was very, it was a sight you'll never forget. The North Koreans had come down during the evening and had caught these Americans by surprise and had practically killed every one of them. The American tanks there were just blown up and the artillery pieces had charges put in the barrels and they were blown up. There were American boys' personal effects lying on the ground, their shavings kits, pictures of things from home. But there was no bodies. There was no evidence of death or anything like that. They'd been all cleaned up. But the aftermath of a battle like that was pretty horrendous and I never did forget it. Q. You never went over to the Pacific during World War 2?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: Not during World War 2. I was on the way over and when I was home on leave between two conflicts, the atomic bomb was dropped.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: On Hiroshima?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: Uh-huh. And so my orders were cancelled and our unit wasn't sent over there.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: And then the second bomb was dropped on Nagasaki?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: Is there anything you'd like to add that we haven't covered or I haven't asked you about, any story you want to tell or anything?

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: There's not much that I can think of that we haven't covered. I just feel that America is worth fighting for and I'm just so happy to see what's happening with our military today. In Iraq it's still the same problem, that we are continuously going to have to fight and stand up for our freedoms. And we have done that a number of times. And we will have to do that in the future.

sp.speaker: Mary J. McGowan
sp.p: Thank you for talking with me.

sp.speaker: W.K. Manchette
sp.p: I'm glad to have done it. Thank you.
[Conclusion of interview]
